item.title: The rise of GLP-1s.
item.dc:creator: Audrey Moorehead
item.description: Plus, the stories we didn’t cover this week.
item.content:encoded:
Today’s topic.

GLP-1s. In recent years, use of new weight-loss medications has risen in the United States. A 2026 Gallup poll found that a record 11% of U.S. adults are taking GLP-1 medications for weight loss, up from 3% in 2024. Furthermore, high-profile figures like Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker (D) and decorated tennis player Serena Williams have extolled their experiences taking the drug. The rising prevalence of GLP-1 use for weight management has sparked a debate over their potential impact on health and wellness in the U.S.

Back up: GLP-1s, or “glucagon-like peptide-1 agonists,” are a class of medication that primarily treats Type 2 diabetes and obesity. GLP-1 agonists mimic the GLP-1 hormone, which is made in the small intestine, to trigger insulin release, slow down digestion, and increase the feeling of fullness after eating. The Food and Drug Administration first approved GLP-1s for medical use in 2005, but their popularity has increased significantly in recent years with the introduction of brand names like Ozempic and Wegovy. 

The rising adoption of GLP-1s has coincided with U.S. obesity rates decreasing from 39.9% in 2022 to 36.8% in 2026. Users like Gov. Pritzker have reported health improvements after lifetime struggles with weight management; Pritzker said he has lost 80 pounds in the two years since he began taking a GLP-1 medication. 

Under current federal law, Medicare and Medicaid mostly cover GLP-1s if prescribed for diabetes, but new initiatives are exploring potential coverage for obesity. In July, Medicare launched a pilot program to provide certain GLP-1s to some Medicare Part D beneficiaries. The Trump administration has sought to negotiate reduced prices for the drugs for Medicare and Medicaid recipients, as well as U.S. consumers paying for them out-of-pocket.

The side effects of the drugs are still being studied, and a March 2026 study by the Washington University School of Medicine found that people who start and then stop GLP-1 treatments experience a “meaningful increase in the risk of major cardiovascular events compared with [those] remaining on the medication.” Another study identified a biological mechanism that may be causing users to regain lost weight after they stop taking the medication. Separately, hundreds of consumers have sued GLP-1 manufacturers Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly, alleging that the drug increases the risk of a condition that causes blindness. 

Today, we’ll share views from the right and left on the rising prevalence of GLP-1s. Then, Editor Audrey Moorehead’s take.

What the right is saying.
  • Many on the right praise the innovation that led to GLP-1s and their benefits.
  • Some argue that government coverage would raise the price of the medication.
  • Others note the potential health consequences of taking the drugs.

The Washington Post editorial board argued “the promise of weight-loss drugs keeps growing.”

“Eli Lilly announced [in May] that the highest dose of its new weight-loss drug helped people shed more than 30 percent of their body weight, on par with gastric bypass surgery,” the board wrote. “Eli Lilly’s innovation promises to unlock surgery-free treatment for people with a severely high body mass index, for whom weight-loss medications have not been a durable option… Studies have found that users of these drugs cut their grocery expenditures.”

“That could mean reducing future health care costs on chronic illnesses such as diabetes and cardiovascular disease,” the board said. “Not long ago, addressing America’s obesity epidemic was seen as something only the government could solve by micromanaging consumers’ eating habits. As is often the case, however, science-based innovation has proven far more effective than any initiative from Washington.”

In National Review, John R. Puri said “don’t ruin GLP-1 prices by having the government cover them.”

“Over the past few years, the American health-care sector has seen a real-time experiment in what happens when a revolutionary treatment runs outside traditional payment systems,” Puri wrote. “Usually, when the FDA approves a new drug, its cost is quickly covered by employer-run insurance plans and the government through Medicare and Medicaid. Yet the makers of GLP-1 drugs, approved for weight loss, have had to compete for patients’ dollars more directly.”

“Individual patients may be annoyed that insurance won’t pick up the tab on a pricey brand-name drug, but the result of widespread self-payment has been vicious price competition to win market share,” Puri said. “The price of GLP-1 drugs will probably keep falling, but only if patients have to pay for the drugs themselves. Governments should limit their appetite for providing short-term relief at long-term expense.”

In the Daily Wire, Benjamin Chacko asked “are we using medicinal drugs to support healthy living, or as a substitute for it?”

“One extreme dismisses GLP-1s as another ‘miracle cure’ sold by Big Pharma. The other imagines that a weekly injection can replace the hard work of building health. Both are false gods,” Chacko wrote. “Disease begins with what we eat, how we sleep, how we move, and a food environment that has been, for decades, making processed calories cheaper, more addictive, and more accessible than real nutrition. The Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement is rightly focused on those upstream causes. 

“GLP-1s should complement that mission, not compete with it,” Chacko said. “Medicine is crossing an important threshold as we develop drugs that will influence motivation, reward, and desire themselves. That is an extraordinary scientific achievement, but it also demands extraordinary wisdom. We know GLP-1s work, but they cannot replace the habits, character, and choices that allow people to flourish. The question at hand is whether we’ll use them to support health or to substitute for it. Those are two very different futures.”

What the left is saying.
  • Many on the left suggest GLP-1s should be treated like any other medicine.
  • Some lament that Americans’ views on weight cause GLP-1 users to feel guilty.
  • Others worry these drugs are exacerbating certain eating disorders.

In New York Magazine, Sarah Jones asked “why can’t we treat GLP-1s like medicine?”

“When I first started taking the drug, I was reluctant to mention it to anyone,” Jones wrote. “Diabetes is complicated enough by itself, and the American health-care system is one more obstacle to good health. In my case, Cigna refused to cover Mounjaro at the lowest dose, which forced me to increase it on corporate timing, not my own or my doctor’s. I hoped it would be all right. The endocrinologist’s nurse told me I might have gastrointestinal symptoms, but the drug was good for my blood sugar and the side effects usually got easier over time. She was right, for a while.”

“I lost nearly a third of my total body weight by April and saw a new endocrinologist, who told me that I’d developed a significant vitamin-D deficiency. I told her I wanted to have children, and she finally took me off Mounjaro,” Jones said. “I don’t know who to blame for any of this… Perhaps I could blame the Reformation, or capitalism, or some unholy combination thereof; the damage is the same. We’ve lost sight of Mounjaro as medicine. A GLP-1 is not snake oil or a miracle drug but a tool, and it can be helpful without being right for every person.”

In Vox, Dylan Scott suggested “Americans still have a toxic relationship with weight.”

“GLP-1 drugs promised to usher in a new era of treating obesity as a disease. We could leave behind the anti-fat biases of the past, which blamed obesity on moral failing or personal weakness,” Scott wrote. “Instead, these drugs would allow us to approach it as a medical condition, a complex matrix of genetics and other forces which could be changed with the right dose of these powerful new medicines. Or so the thinking went.” 

“Even as millions of Americans shed pounds in bulk for the first time, they are also contending with fierce stigma and shaming from others — instead of being criticized for being fat, they are being criticized for using GLP-1s,” Scott said. “Americans have internalized the message that being overweight is a personal failure so thoroughly that… many people struggle to see [the availability of these drugs] as good news. They see it as cheating.”

In The New York Times, Jessica Grose suggested “GLP-1s feed our sick culture.”

“Multiple things can be true about GLP-1s: They are truly miracles and may treat a whole range of conditions beyond obesity and diabetes. And they are often misused, partly because we have told women in multiple ways that being thin makes them valuable,” Grose wrote. “As my colleague Tressie McMillan Cottom has written, our culture ‘makes being fat a woman’s burden, a means test for dignity, work, social status and moral citizenry.’”

“[In a recent JAMA Psychiatry study,] researchers found that the use and misuse of GLP-1s is higher among people with eating disorders than among the general population and that some of them may be attempting to maintain their ‘eating disorder psychopathology through rapid restriction and weight loss.’ They found that over 10% of participants with anorexia had tried GLP-1s,” Grose said. “Though GLP-1s may be a promising treatment for some kinds of disordered eating, like binge-eating disorder, it appears much riskier for women with other kinds of diagnoses.”

My take.
Audrey Moorehead
Editor
 
 
  • The benefits of GLP-1s are increasingly apparent: lower obesity rates, improved health outcomes, and less strain on public health. 
  • But the prevalence of the drugs also raises difficult questions about cultural norms on appearance.
  • I considered taking GLP-1s, but opted for diet and exercise first; that choice has been effective and fulfilling.
Reminder: This is where we share a personal opinion. If you have feedback, criticism or compliments, leave a comment or reply to this email.

In this era of hyperpartisan polarization, which is now affecting the conversation on weight-loss drugs of all things, it’s important to remember: The internet is not real life. Issues are not flat and two-dimensional. In the real world, where the sky is brilliant blue and the air smells of crisp leaves and your body fat (wherever it may be) jiggles while you walk, multiple things can be true at once.

First and foremost — as with many new medical technologies — GLP-1s are a net good for American public health. It’s hard to argue otherwise. From 2017–2020, nearly 42% of U.S. adults over 20 were obese, increasing their risk of serious chronic health problems like heart disease and diabetes. According to the CDC, obesity-related issues and treatments accounted for $173 billion (in 2019 dollars) of annual healthcare costs. And a study from the 2010s found that obesity-related deaths increased from 1.8 per 100,000 people in 2010 to 3.1 per 100,000 in 2020. In short, before the advent of Ozempic, obesity was one of the leading — if not the leading — health issues facing Americans, and things were getting worse, not better. In my mind, then, a new set of drugs that relieves the worst of this public health crisis is an unquestionable good for the world.

But, as is the case with many new medical technologies, GLP-1s aren’t a magic wand we can wave to fix the culture that produced an obesity epidemic; and because weight loss and weight gain are often a game of extremes, it’s fair to question whether these drugs will swing the pendulum to the other dangerous end. It’s disappointing, but not surprising, to see that these concerns have ended up divided along partisan lines. 

Under today’s “What the right is saying” section, Benjamin Chacko points to the “Make America Healthy Again” movement and its concern that GLP-1s change problematic behaviors that produce obesity but don’t change problematic mindsets. The thinking goes that the drug might reduce a person's desire for food in the short term, but it doesn’t adequately address the twisted relationships to food Americans might have. Frankly, I’m sympathetic to fears that disconnecting unhealthy actions and thought processes from their consequences can exacerbate, rather than cure, societal dysfunction. It’s a long-game assertion, hard to measure when GLP-1s are so new, but we’ve seen it happen in other spheres. 

Look at the problem of grade inflation. Studies from the ’80s showed that students who receive poor grades can be discouraged from learning, turning the students who most need more instruction away from education. So, educators started grading more gently. But when teachers give students higher grades than their work might otherwise deserve, students get a short-term boost but ultimately have lower lifetime outcomes. Isn’t it possible that the same handicapping might be true of giving people with unhealthy habits access to a miracle drug that suppresses their desire for food? Many GLP-1 users regain the weight once they stop using the drugs, which signals early support for that hypothesis from the right.

The left (including Jessica Grose in “What the left is saying” today), in the spirit of body positivity, fears that GLP-1s are ushering in a new wave of eating disorders and reckless pursuits of an imagined ideal of thinness. One only needs to read about how GLP-1s have exacerbated the already-harmful parts of sorority culture — prompting girls of such gargantuan proportions as size 8 in dresses to call up their moms for the shots — to understand that this fear is well founded. 

Even more disturbing is that many Americans who can’t get their doctor to prescribe peptides are turning to “gray market” drugs with no FDA approval or medical oversight. This in particular alarms me: When Americans order drugs from overseas, there’s no way to ensure they’re getting what they’re ordering, and it’s harder to ensure that the drugs are prepared and dosed safely. Sure enough, some people have experienced side effects after taking illicit GLP-1s, and regulators have found that purported vials of the unapproved drug retatrutide have sometimes contained very different ingredients. If Americans are willing to risk taking unproven mystery drugs just to lose a few pounds, is that really a sign of a culture primarily concerned with health?

The culture of GLP-1s isn’t a zero-sum game — both fears of personal and societal degradation can be true at once. In fact, if GLP-1s have had any impact on the culture so far, it’s been to force a reckoning with how Americans think about our weight and health. I’m not exactly watching this story at a remove. In fact, I almost feel as though my life is a microcosm of many Americans’ relationship with weight, and GLP-1s have forced me to confront my own habits and lifestyle as much as anything else.

I won’t go so far as to say I’ve always struggled with my weight. I spent most of elementary, middle and high school blessedly average, despite being decidedly inactive and not really watching what I ate. But in college, to deal with the stress of moving far away from home, taking difficult classes and struggling to make new friends, I turned to food as a coping mechanism. When I started gaining weight, I didn’t stop to reflect on whether I had a problem; I assumed that obesity couldn’t just “happen” to me. But, slowly and surely, and without me noticing, it did. Even after I’d resolved the emotional stresses that led me to adopt bad habits, the bad habits stuck around, and I wasn’t paying attention to them.

When GLP-1s first came out, I was still in denial about problems with my weight, even as I noticed that I was struggling to take long walks or get up stairs. But as people around me began using the drugs — some privately, some more openly — I felt curious. I wasn’t obese, I thought (though I was), but sure, I could stand to lose a few pounds. Would it be so bad to take a drug to get those off? And suddenly, I was paying attention to how I looked in the mirror, or in photos. For the first time in my life, I really felt self-conscious about how I appeared, and that self-consciousness prompted me to probe my physical health. After all, I was young and supposed to be in the prime of my life, but somehow, exercise was a struggle. 

I don’t remember who brought it up first, me or my friend using gray-market retatrutide, but I remember the night I ended up scrolling through the website they used, looking at vials and needles and dosage sizes. I asked my friend how the injections worked, and they dutifully assured me that swabbing and jabbing my skin would be easy. But at that description, I chickened out: There was no way I could stab myself with a needle when I had to psych myself up just to get a flu shot. I thanked them for the links and the info and said I might try it later. Instead, I called up my brother (a bona fide fitness nerd) and asked him about losing weight the old-fashioned way; I told myself if diet and exercise failed, I could fall back on the drugs.

To my surprise, I discovered I did have the willpower to keep up with the diet, and the rewards of getting back to a healthy weight created a self-perpetuating motivation cycle. I only dealt with constant food cravings for a couple of weeks before the “food noise” subsided permanently; and when I ate too much while at dinner with friends, I could snap back to discipline the next day. But not everyone has the same experience. Some people’s cravings never subside, and even just one night off-track can feel like it resets all their progress. I don’t experience that with food, but I do experience it in other areas of my life where I’ve tried and failed to curb bad habits on my own before (like managing screen time). So I can’t begrudge the use of GLP-1s for people for whom food is a constant temptation — especially when the alternative is untreated obesity.

Beginning to lose weight forced me, for the first time, to confront the culture I’d ingested since I was a teenager. I grew up on Instagram, Tumblr, and Twitter at the peak of the body-positivity movement. Influencers’ and activists’ attempts to raise eating-disorder awareness and discourage body comparison were well founded and well meaning, and I took them to heart as a teen. Being overweight wouldn’t make me a bad person or worth less than anyone else. But they never mentioned that it would mean I was more susceptible to illness and injury, or less capable of physical activity than other people.

At the same time, the rise of GLP-1s has brought back the “skinny culture” that body positivity was created to resist, and I’ve learned that you can’t put the self-awareness genie back in the bottle. Once I became aware of my weight, I became hyperaware of it — perpetually conscious of my own imperfections. And in some ways, “skinny culture” is even worse now that people can use drugs to lose weight, because it now comes with the added moralizing dimension of how you become and stay skinny, not just whether you do.

It’s hard to say what the ultimate solution to this problem even is, when the healthy-weight conversation seems to constantly oscillate between the two extremes of “you’re healthy at any weight” and “you’re only healthy at a very specific weight in a very specific way.” But I think it probably requires walking a path between those extremes. Obsessing over being skinny and looking a certain way is unhealthy, and learning not to hang your self-worth on your physical appearance is vitally important for your mental and physical health. However, obesity is also unhealthy, and finding a solution — whether it’s the diet plan that has worked for me or the GLP-1s that have worked for others — is vitally important for your mental and physical health. 

Oddly, I’m hopeful that the rise of GLP-1s, with their extreme short-term effects, will balance things out in the long run. I’m also hopeful that the attempts to stigmatize GLP-1s are just the last gasp of a moralizing weight-loss culture finally dying out — and that in its place, a culture that can stop thinking so much about food and weight will arise.

Staff dissent.
Isaac Saul
Executive Editor
 
I agree with Audrey that GLP-1 use is a great choice for some people and will likely improve overall health throughout American society. Yet I can’t shake the concern that GLP-1s are the latest rung on the ladder to a frictionless life. The AI chatbots do our thinking, the influencers summarize our news in one-minute videos, and GLP-1s shed our weight. There’s no need to read, think critically, research, or exercise anymore. There’s very little discipline. Shoot, even the bikes are now electric and do our pedaling.
 
I have no idea if GLP-1s will have some long-term, unseen downside, but given how many parts of our lives they impact, I suspect they will (people’s personalities are known to change, as well as other non-food-related habits; heart rates also increase, and we don’t yet fully understand any of this). I have a hard time finding GLP-1s encouraging in that larger context, and am inherently skeptical of any so-called “miracle drug.”
 
But I mostly find myself worried about how few challenges people are overcoming on their own anymore.
 

Take the survey: What is your relationship to GLP-1s? Let us know.

Disagree? That’s okay. Our opinion is just one of many. Write in and let us know why, and we’ll consider publishing your feedback.

item.title: The U.S.–Greenland Deal.
item.dc:creator: Carina Pacheco
item.description: How big of a deal is it?
item.content:encoded:
Today’s topic.

The Greenland deal. On Tuesday, President Donald Trump signed a defense agreement with Denmark and the semiautonomous territory of Greenland. The three-party compact was signed in New York City, concurrent with a United Nations General Assembly meeting, and it follows several months of statements from President Trump about the United States increasing its control over the island territory. 

Back up: In his first term, President Trump proposed buying Greenland and has returned to the idea in his second, citing the territory’s vast natural resources and its strategic geographic positioning for trade and national security. In January, Trump escalated his efforts to acquire the island, explicitly declining to rule out the potential to use force and threatening to impose tariffs on European nations that opposed the move. Denmark’s and Greenland’s leaders have rebuffed the president’s efforts to acquire the territory.

Trump announced the agreement on Friday, saying on social media that it would give the United States “permanent control” over Greenland’s security and “other needs.” The deal extends the United States’s existing authority on the island, with new specifications that allow the U.S. to build more military bases and forbids any non-NATO state from military or civilian investment without U.S. approval. Additionally, the text of the deal specifies that the agreement would remain in place if Greenland declares independence from Denmark, should the territory decide to pursue it.

Denmark and the United States have had a defense agreement over Greenland dating back to 1951, which allows the U.S. to build and maintain military bases on the island, while giving Denmark sovereign control. The U.S. currently operates one base in Greenland, Pituffik Space Base in the northwest, which has roughly 150 personnel. 

At the agreement’s signing, President Trump said the deal will lead to a “tremendous relationship” between the three parties. “We will have the complete ability to do what is necessary to defend the American continent and also Europe and other places,” he said. “No U.S. adversary will ever be permitted to establish a military presence in Greenland anymore.”

Critics of the deal said that President Trump incurred significant diplomatic costs in pursuing the agreement. Torrey Taussig of the Atlantic Council said it is “unlikely to quiet concerns European allies have over America's broader commitment to [NATO].”

We’ll get into what the left and right are saying about the deal below. Then, Associate Editor Carina Pacheco gives her take.

What the left is saying.
  • Many on the left say that Trump could have secured this arrangement without his political theatre. 
  • Some argue that the deal came at great cost to America’s global standing. 
  • Others suggest the agreement doesn’t accomplish the president’s stated goals.

In USA Today, Chris Brennan suggested the president “could’ve had this Greenland agreement all along.”

“As always, Trump's announcement ran long on bluster and short on details. Here's the part he left out — everything Trump now claims as a win was available to him 20 months ago on the very first day of his second term,” Brennan wrote. “It was also available for Trump during his first term, when he floated the idea of buying Greenland before threatening to take it by force in his second term after his threats were rebuffed by Greenland and Denmark. 

“Greenland and Denmark have existing, non-expiring security agreements and treaties that have always allowed for an American military expansion in Greenland, the world's largest island, which has significant strategic value in the Arctic Circle,” Brennan said. “Trump's rhetoric about Greenland has been all braggadocio and bombast. That has destabilized America's relationship not just with Greenland and Denmark but across Europe and around the world… Trump is trying to sell an embarrassment as a win.”

In The Atlantic, Isaac Stanley-Becker said the deal “appeared to satisfy all parties but came at a great cost.”

“The promised ‘future deal’ appears to be here. It builds on a Cold War agreement between the U.S. and Denmark and includes no transfer of territory to the United States,” Stanley-Becker wrote. “Instead, it envisions the kind of expanded U.S.-military access and multilateral cooperation that leaders from Denmark and Greenland said was available all along, and doesn’t threaten to blow up the security architecture that the U.S. has helped maintain for nearly 80 years.”

“The new agreement will also include Greenland and bind all three parties to a more permanent U.S. presence,” Stanley-Becker said. “[Statements from Greenland and Denmark leaders] were positive but restrained, reflecting the pain inflicted by this saga. Europeans found it difficult to decipher Trump’s motives — or to understand whether they were about to be attacked or simply trolled… Washington may have achieved its security objectives. But it has lost something else: trust among its hosts.”

The Economist argued “the harm has been done.”

“The arctic is a safer place for America and its allies today. Due credit must go to President Donald Trump,” the writer said. “In these cynical times, it is a relief when war-talk turns out to be bluster, but not grounds for a medal. By Mr. Trump’s own previously stated standards, the deal falls short… He has settled for what amount to reworded lease terms, with demands for ownership quietly dropped. Mr. Trump calls the new agreement a ‘dream come true’ for America, which he says now controls Greenland’s security and ‘all other needs’ in perpetuity. 

“There will be no cost to America as it develops a ‘large military presence’ in Greenland, he adds. It remains unclear what he means by that, for Denmark, a country of 6 million people, is not about to foot the whole bill for America’s Arctic garrison,” the writer said. “America’s desire for Arctic bases (and Europe’s need for American help to deter Russia) resolved this particular presidential tantrum. But gibes asking why America should defend foreign soil cannot be unsaid. The transatlantic bond is growing colder and far more transactional. Mr. Trump wanted Greenland to be part of his legacy and so it will be. Just not as he imagined."

What the right is saying.
  • The right is mixed, with some saying the agreement again proves Trump’s dealmaking ability. 
  • Others praise the deal for addressing national security concerns.
  • Still others accuse the president of misunderstanding the interests of other nations.

The Washington Times editorial board wrote “Trump cement[ed] his status as master dealmaker.”

“Initially, the president spoke of the United States taking over the world’s largest island. That led to accusations of gunboat diplomacy. Mr. Trump’s critics missed his modus operandi, which usually starts with the big ask and then settles for something more modest and achievable,” the board said. “Greenland’s strategic importance cannot be overstated. Control of Greenland affects control of the Arctic. Whoever controls the Arctic will probably win a future world war.” 

“The deal is a win all the way around. Denmark could never hope to defend the territory from a hostile takeover bid. Greenland is vital to America’s security interests, and Greenlanders need help extracting their valuable mineral reserves. As important as getting America in is keeping Russia and China out. There can be no doubt of the hostile intentions of either nation,” the board wrote. “For either hostile power to secure a foothold in Greenland would be disastrous. Mr. Trump’s masterful deal precludes that.”

In UnHerd, Tom Rogan suggested the agreement will offer “protection against foreign threats.”

“It strongly appears that Trump has abandoned his always-foolish demand that Greenland be brought under American sovereign control. That demand was incompatible with America’s moral obligation to support the will of free peoples, and its political obligation to Nato allies,” Rogan wrote. “While this concord could have been reached with far less acrimony earlier in the Trump administration (existing agreements with Denmark already grant the US military extensive access to Greenland), it still represents a positive development. 

“There is no question, after all, that Russia and China pose significant and growing threats in the Arctic High North. These nations seek to exploit the region’s natural resources and expand their Arctic military footprints,” Rogan said. “These ambitions are intolerable from an American perspective, and Friday’s deal helps address these concerns by facilitating a rapid, wide-ranging U.S. military buildup. That presence will boost the U.S. military’s freedom of action and increase Nato deterrence credibility… This agreement provides a mutually beneficial resolution to a contentious issue.”

National Review’s editors called the saga “Trump’s costly Greenland play.”

“To be clear, Trump was right about one big thing: that Greenland merited much more attention than it had been getting… The island is a potential back door through U.S. defenses and a key North Atlantic vantage point,” the editors wrote. “Given the limited resources Denmark has at its disposal to defend Greenland, an agreement to upgrade the U.S. presence needed doing… Asking politely to upgrade the existing agreement might well have delivered just that — and done so without creating all the geopolitical self-harm. 

“Unfortunately, Trump went about defending the U.S. strategic interest in a different way, and that was the wrong way. The core of the problem has been that, despite his own nationalist instincts, the president is oblivious when it comes to the national sensitivities of others,” the editors said. “If and when an agreement is concluded, the best way to maximize its benefits to the U.S. will be to repair the diplomatic damage that this episode has caused by rebuilding a deeper relationship with Denmark and Greenland.”

My take.
Carina Pacheco
Associate Editor
 
  • The Greenland saga is a reminder to take Trump seriously but not literally.
  • We saw this with NATO, when his threats to back out successfully pushed member nations into stronger commitments.
  • Now Trump has strengthened our ties with Greenland and NATO, securing a deal that improves our national security.
Reminder: This is where we share a personal opinion. If you have feedback, criticism or compliments, leave a comment on the website or reply to this email.

When President Trump announced the deal between the United States, Greenland and Denmark, I was taken aback. I’d almost completely forgotten about the semiautonomous island, but sure enough, one utterance and the memories of Trumpian threats of invasion and annexation all came flooding back.

It reminded me of a very important lesson that we’ve been hearing about the president for a long time: take Trump seriously, not literally. 

Now, I admit that it would be nice to be able to take a president both literally and seriously, and to not have to guess which of his statements should be taken at face value. But alas, we live in interesting times, and the defining political character of the century is a showman by trade. If the past decade-plus has taught us anything, it’s that we have to put up with a little… drama.

This administration’s foreign policy has a recurring pattern: Trump puts out an outlandish, maximalist demand, which is met with an outsized emotional reaction from his political opponents. Behind the scenes, negotiations and deliberations ensue, and the end result is much more “normal” than the original, more absurd demand. The left decries the process that got us to the end result and laments the embarrassment they feel about our president, while Trump’s supporters focus on the wins in the deal and mock the left for overreacting. Rinse. Repeat. 

To illustrate my point, let’s look at Trump’s relationship with NATO. 

Trump has scrutinized the U.S.’s outsized NATO spending since the ’80s, and that rhetoric has been present in each of his presidential campaigns. He charged other member nations with “ripping off” the U.S. with delinquent payments and even hinted at the possibility of not defending NATO allies if they hadn’t “fulfilled their obligations.” He doubled down on that possibility during his first term, and even suggested that he would withdraw the U.S. from the alliance (which would require approval from Congress). 

Trump’s grievances are well founded: The U.S. has been financing the alliance’s defenses at disproportionate levels, accounting for approximately 66% of total NATO spending in 2024. Of course, that’s partially due to our significantly larger economy, but many member nations have historically skimped on the 2014 pledge to contribute at least 2% of their GDP. I’m speculating here, but I’m sure our media-focused president wasn’t taking too kindly to allies criticizing him in the press, bragging about their national social safety nets, then relying on the good old American military safety net for their continental security. If I were Trump, I’d be pretty sick of the geopolitical version of “for breakfast we’ll do something cool like have a cigarette then like a bar of chocolate, then we go to work for like one half hour, two half hour” — especially when my country’s taxpayers were subsidizing their national security.

In his second term, Trump continued a campaign of rhetoric against his NATO allies. He publicly criticized low-spending members, leveraged his threats to not honor NATO's collective defense principle, and teased withdrawing from the alliance completely. By last year, all 32 members had complied. This is no small feat, considering that only five members met the 2% target in the last pre-Trump year of 2016 (and only 11 met it in 2023, the year following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine). At the 2025 NATO Summit, the alliance formally adopted a 5% of GDP target for 2035 — also a Trump proposal. 

I suspect Trump’s threats to leave NATO were a negotiating tactic and not something he’d ever follow through on; nor do I think the U.S. would ever fail to come to the aid of an ally. But the upside of Trump’s maximalist strategy is that you never really know, which makes him a difficult but imposing negotiating partner. This maximalist strategy has certainly bruised some relationships and garnered plenty of negative press that the president might pay for politically, but with NATO he got what he wanted: a stronger shared defense budget. So the two worst-case outcomes were avoided; we’re still in NATO, and everyone is contributing more money. Kumbaya, right? 

Trump proved that his maximalism and unpredictability are powerful forms of leverage. And that leverage is heightened further by the sensationalist tendencies of the mainstream media, which often ignores the contextual pattern that any clear-eyed Trump-watcher could see coming a mile away. I understand this dynamic creates tension for the media whose job it is to report on the president, but how many more examples are required to understand how Trump operates? I liken his approach to an angry teenager slamming the door and yelling, “I’m running away!” — it’s always less of an actual plan and more of an opening bid designed to extract maximum concessions. Treating Trump's theatrical tendencies as incompetence and lunacy misses most of the story. 

That brings us back to Greenland — that big, beautiful icy island with its wonderful colorful houses and immensely strategic geopolitical positioning. 

Trump had shown interest in Greenland in his first term, but American presidential interest in acquiring the territory dates back to at least 1946. Just after the Second World War and at the start of the Cold War, President Harry S. Truman proposed buying Greenland outright. Denmark promptly rejected his $100 million offer.

The island is the last piece of the puzzle that encircles the Arctic, along with North America, Northern Europe, and Russia. It sits at a vital marine intersection and is rich in rare earth minerals. Russia and China are striving to assert dominance in the Arctic by developing military bases, research ships and energy initiatives in the region, edging up against Alaska, Scandinavia, and Greenland. 

In late 2024, then-President-elect Trump declared that “the ownership and control of Greenland is an absolute necessity” for “National Security and Freedom throughout the World.” Then, in the first joint address to Congress of his second term, Trump did not mince words when he said that the U.S. will achieve that control “one way or the other.” A few months later, Trump refused to rule out the use of military force. 

The media — as well as the leaders of Greenland, Denmark, and NATO — took Trump very literally. 

And of course, when taken literally, the threats — to invade a sparsely populated ally that’s also technically a member of NATO — were bizarre. But these Trumpisms, at least to me, were transparent — a negotiation tool rather than a real threat — and I would have thought, over 10 years into the Trump era, that others, too, would learn to exercise some discretion when analyzing his Truth Social posts. Though the U.S. has owned and operated a military base in Greenland since 1951, Trump believed we needed an increased military presence to address the perceived threats from adversaries — Greenland is simply too strategically imperative to risk. 

To state the obvious, Trump’s chaotic strategy was not bulletproof. He lost political capital and may, at least to the literalists, look like he “settled” for a deal he had initially approached much more aggressively. But his strategy ultimately paid off. 

If we look at this deal in terms of the end result, instead of what was threatened along the way, here’s what we come to: The U.S. gets expansive, exclusive rights to stand up and expand new military installations; Greenland’s companies are promised first looks for any contracted work; and Washington wields explicit authority to approve or block foreign investments in Greenland's rare earth minerals. And if Greenland ever does become independent, the deal already approves a continuation of the U.S.–Greenland agreements and locks the new government into NATO. From the signing on Tuesday, it appears that each participant is happy with the end result, making it an even more reassuring outcome for the U.S., Greenland, Denmark, and NATO alike — but we’ll all have to suspend our disbelief when Trump doesn’t describe it modestly on Truth Social.

Staff dissent.
Ari Weitzman
Managing Editor
 
 
I’ll acknowledge two biases up front, and maybe they cancel each other out: First, I used to work for NATO as a lowly Library Intern at an educational facility in Rome, Italy, when I was 23. Second, I just love reading and editing Carina’s work; she really convincingly argues why concern over this saga was overwrought from the start.
 
But I don’t think that’s quite true. When you look at how Trump’s maximalist, constantly shifting foreign policy threats play elsewhere, you see externalities everywhere: China investing in South America, Russia investing in Africa, chaos engulfing the Middle East.
 
To me, the whole game is in the conclusion that Trump’s gambit “ultimately paid off.” If you draw a tight perimeter around all the costs and benefits in this story as they relate to the outcome of the Greenland deal, then the ends may justify the means. But not when you consider the externalities. Military and economic allies don’t typically love being antagonized, and the recent news of the European Union offering Canada “associate membership” in their alliance signals that the Western Democratic Order is reconsidering whether the U.S. is too erratic to count on as a partner.
 
The U.S. got a somewhat better agreement with Greenland than the one we already had. That’s great. But will our alliance be strong and ready if and when we may call upon it to aid us? I hope we don’t need to find out, but I’m less confident in that now. What I am confident in, though, is that this deal is not where the story ends.

Take the survey: What do you think of the deal? Let us know.

Disagree? That’s okay. Our opinion is just one of many. Write in and let us know why, and we’ll consider publishing your feedback.

Under the radar.

On Monday, the Federal Aviation Administration launched an initiative to leverage artificial intelligence to address protracted challenges with air-traffic control. The $875 million software overhaul will install the Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (SMART) system, which will use AI to survey planned airline flights, weather, wind, and other variables to suggest flight-schedule changes to mitigate the risk of delays. SMART will first be deployed at the three major airports in the Washington, D.C. region, with plans to expand in the near future. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the system will make airline operations more efficient and lower the cost of flying. Separately, the National Air Traffic Controllers Association has yet to take a stance on SMART, saying in a statement that it “has not been involved in the design, testing, or implementation of SMART and therefore cannot speak to its effect on the air traffic control workforce at this time.” NPR has the story.

By Isaac Saul, Executive Editor, Tangle Founder

Let me start with an obvious point that everyone should grant: News organizations don’t have a First Amendment right to just walk into the White House. 

The Trump administration — and its defenders — are correct when they argue that covering the White House as part of the press pool is a privilege, not a right. However frustrating the president’s messaging, these organizations aren’t having their rights infringed solely by being denied presidential access. I’m the leader of a news organization, and I’ve been reporting on national politics for 15 years, yet all my applications for a White House press pass have been denied. I don’t automatically get access to the president just because I’m a member of the media. 

So yes, a White House press pass is a privilege; you have to apply, be accepted into the press pool, and follow the rules once you’re inside. There is a reason the room is populated by the biggest news organizations in the world. 

However, that doesn’t mean this move is fair or even legal. Revoking a news organization’s access based on the content of their reporting is almost certainly a form of viewpoint discrimination, which is a violation of the First Amendment. The Trump administration may also be violating their due process and property rights under the Fifth Amendment, which is exactly the grounds on which news organizations are now suing the Trump administration. I suspect, too, that those outlets will win their lawsuits on the merits, especially since the Trump-appointed judge assigned to the case has shown a keen deference toward press freedom in the past.

So, yes: The White House gets to choose who’s in the room. But they don’t get to revoke access for people or organizations because they don’t like their coverage. That tug of war between the federal government and the media is well established, and it’s something we should all be grateful for. 

What counts as a “hoax”?

Which brings me to the White House’s defense of this move. In response to CNN posting a statement about the ban, the White House Rapid Response team posted a graphic of purported CNN “hoaxes” over the years:

The graphic is actually instructive as a look into how the White House thinks about past reporting and what it deems “fake” and “real” news. Very few of these stories were actually hoaxes — that is, totally fictional accounts — save examples like Jussie Smollett faking his own racially charged attack (which was something CNN reported on with insufficient skepticism, not a myth the outlet itself created from whole cloth). But within Trump’s orbit, the definition of the word hoax has morphed into anything from “story published with inaccuracies” to “exaggerated or misleading story.” And it’s true CNN has had some whoppers over the years. 

The “Covington Kids” story was reported with so much bias as to obscure the reality of what happened, and CNN paid the price for it. Claims that Trump promised a “bloodbath” if he lost the election were intentionally quoted out of context to make it seem like he was promising a civil war rather than warning that the auto industry would fail without him. Kyle Rittenhouse was never driven across state lines by his mother, and he did not illegally transport a rifle across state lines, both inaccurate claims CNN reported. Trump never called for Liz Cheney to be executed, but he did insist she stand on the front lines of a war before sending our kids off to fight it for us (this was before Trump launched the Iran war). Other times, CNN leaned into a technically true framing — like the fact that Kamala Harris was never technically border czar — that obscured the truth so much as to be misleading. 

I have written or tweeted about most of this inaccurate or misleading reporting in the past, and all of these mistakes always seem to go in one direction. CNN is deserving of criticism for its consistent and demonstrated anti-Trump bias, and the White House is well within its rights to use its bullhorn to call it out.  

At the same time, a lot of the purported “hoaxes” in the graphic are real things that happened that CNN and other outlets reported accurately. David DePape, the man who assaulted Paul Pelosi, was a die-hard Trump supporter. And after the assault, many in the MAGA world — including Trump’s own son — mocked Pelosi for being brutally beaten by one of their own supporters. That isn’t a hoax. Trump did run for re-election while promising to pursue death penalties again, and he has since pushed for reinstating firing squads. This, too, is not a hoax. Israeli troops did, actually, shoot and kill food-seeking Palestinians at an aid site. Also not a hoax. And Melania Trump’s documentary was a box office flop, earning just over $16 million after Amazon spent $40 million to buy it. You guessed it — not a hoax. 

CNN was right to report that Biden never banned gas stoves and never pushed for such a ban. All that he did was appoint a commissioner on the independent Consumer Product Safety Commission who called gas stoves a “hidden hazard” and said “any option is on the table” in an interview, which conservative columnists then wrote about as Biden planning to ban gas stoves. Biden never planned to do such a thing, and immediately responded to the comments by saying he had no such plans. It was a rather silly story that got blown way out of proportion, and under the Trump administration’s definition, it’s actually an example of a conservative media-led “hoax.” 

Trump has offered other justifications for the ban, like claiming Politico was awarded some kind of untoward contract by the federal government as a quid pro quo arrangement for favorable coverage. This claim is also a lie, one that I wrote about at the time in a piece for The Free Press. 

Does bias justify a ban?

Some of Trump’s allies have offered their own defense, arguing — for example — that past administrations have limited access to certain members of the press. Many of these examples are deliberately misleading — like the case of an African journalist named Simon Ateba being “barred” by the Biden administration when, actually, he was denied a permanent hard pass but granted a day pass every time he requested one. 

Other defenders of the president argue that he has a right to ban these outlets because of their bias. “Reporters covering White House briefings should be conveying facts, not spin,” Ward Clark wrote in RedState. Ironically, if that’s true, then RedState’s own press credentials for the Pentagon and White House should be revoked immediately, given that — as their name implies — they are a news organization whose agenda is explicitly aligned with Trump’s.

Quotes like Clark’s make it exceedingly clear how silly and dangerous this all is. Every administration has its critics and allies in the press; this has been true since the Washington administration, and it should be true going forward. None have ever done what Trump is attempting to do now. Bias is in the eye of the beholder, which is precisely why nobody should support an administration banning news outlets it deems as biased — even if they have a track record of mistakes. All that does is ensure future administrations will further restrict press access they don’t like, which is a loss for anyone who believes in free exchange. 

Get more of the story...
We broke down the ban with just the facts, and then we picked out the best arguments from conservative, progressive, and independent writers in today's free newsletter so you can make up your own mind. Read them here. 

What is Trump getting out of this?

It’s astonishing to me that the administration thinks this is the play right now. Yes, the media — writ large — is distrusted by the public and obsessed with itself and will inevitably devote plenty of coverage to its own lawsuits and fights with the administration. I’m sure some of them will even build subscription drives off the battle. That’s their right, and maybe Trump is just betting that CNN, MS NOW and Politico will spend more time on “resistance” navel-gazing and less time critically reporting on actual stories about his administration. 

But the knock-on effects are already breaking against him. Yesterday, the administration held an event so Trump could unveil his new helipad, but there was no audio on the televised event because there was no press pool after the other four networks, including Fox News, banded with CNN and against the ban. It was actually really encouraging to see Fox News's Washington bureau chief condemn the ban during his time as chair of the broadcasting consortium — a reminder that, despite our perceptions of these organizations as partisan warriors, they still lean on traditions of collegiality and mutual respect.

Hours later, Trump launched “Trump TV,” a 24/7 streaming show on the White House YouTube channel that purports to play the greatest hits of his administration, live updates, and breaking news. When I checked the channel out this morning, there was a grand total of 934 people watching a re-run of a Trump rally — and commenting was prohibited. This is the same administration that promised to “restore free speech.”

Meanwhile, back in the real world

Really consider the context here: Gas and diesel prices are both significantly higher than they were when Biden left office, and rising. We’re still stuck in the Iran War, which is now spreading. The Russia–Ukraine war rages on. Inflation is higher today than it was when Biden left office. The number of uninsured Americans has gone up since Biden left office. The native-born employment rate is stagnant. Real wage gains are down, too. There is no long-promised healthcare bill, no election reform bill, no immigration reform bill. The House was just sent home after doing a grand total of four months of work this year because they didn’t want to take a tough vote on impeaching Trump’s secretary of Defense. Now, they won’t be back until after the midterms. 

If any of this concerns you, don’t worry; President Trump is focusing his time on what matters. He just got a new helipad at the White House. He’s hard at work building his ballroom and fighting to get his name on the Kennedy Center (or knock it down), and he’s got plans to turn his grand arch into a drone-deploying military station. And now, thankfully, he’s banned three news organizations from the White House who post stories he doesn’t like, which will inevitably result in taxpayer money being used to fight lawsuits from those organizations that he will very likely lose. 

If this is how the president thinks he can stave off a midterm blowout — or rescue his quickly sinking approval ratings — then the bubble he’s living in is farther removed from reality than I even thought. That’s bad news for Trump, worse news for us, and a much bigger deal than any of the shoddy reporting we’ve all had to live through over the last decade.

Today’s topic.

The White House press bans. On Friday, President Donald Trump announced he is barring journalists from CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House. The president accused the outlets of inaccurately reporting on his administration and suggested that additional news organizations could be banned. On Monday, the outlets sued the government for allegedly violating their First Amendment rights.

In a Truth Social post on Friday, Trump wrote, “Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America.” On Monday, he said the ban was not “an assault on the Free Press” but “an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America.”

On Saturday, CNN, MS NOW, and Politico reporters shared that they had been blocked from entering the White House grounds and had their press passes confiscated. In a Monday statement, the outlets announced they have filed a lawsuit against the ban “to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes.” The organizations are seeking an injunction to pause the ban’s enforcement and restore their journalists’ access to the White House. 

CNN, along with ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC, is a member of the White House television press pool, which provides broadcast coverage of the president. The networks share the costs and duties of reporting from the White House, and with CNN barred from the grounds, the pool announced they will stop providing televised coverage of President Trump while the press ban is in place. Bryan Boughton, the Washington Bureau Chief at Fox News Channel and current acting chair of the pool, said that the decision “follow[ed] the White House’s position preventing CNN from fulfilling its assigned pool duties.”

On Monday evening, the White House announced the launch of “Trump TV,” a streaming channel that will share “top videos, major remarks, and must-see highlights” from the Trump administration. 

Below are perspectives from the right and left on the bans, followed by Executive Editor Isaac Saul’s take.

What the right is saying.
  • The right is mixed, with some arguing the ban does not violate the First Amendment.
  • Others say Trump took the wrong approach to a legitimate problem.
  • Still others predict the president’s action will not hold up in court.

In American Thinker, Andrea Widburg said Trump is “targeting coverage that has… consistently erred.” 

“The mainstream media instantly insisted that Trump was violating the First Amendment,” Widburg wrote. “Since the Constitution doesn’t mention an inherent right to be in the White House to report on and comment on the news of the day, that argument is invalid. As I see it, the only colorable basis for the media’s fight is to claim illegal viewpoint discrimination. That is, that these outlets are being kicked out because they oppose Trump and his policies.

“However, Trump never said that they were being kicked out because they disagreed with him. Indeed, there is no indication that he’s globally blocking any political opponents from access to the White House. Instead, he made a specific allegation about these outlets, which is that they have engaged in knowingly dishonest reporting,” Widburg said. “In sum, the White House position is that it’s not kicking out newsrooms that disagree with Trump. It’s kicking out newsrooms that lie to destroy Trump.”

In PJ Media, Matt Margolis suggested Trump didn’t pick “the smartest way to fix [the problem].”

“Let’s be honest here. The First Amendment doesn’t entitle any media outlet access to the White House grounds. Not every outlet gets a press pass, and that’s never had anything to do with freedom of the press,” Margolis wrote. “You don’t have to try too hard to find examples of these outlets pushing fake news. And let’s be honest here, I don’t even think MS NOW pretends to practice journalism.”

“There’s nothing wrong with journalists being critical of a president. That’s the job. But the job is to report the news accurately, not promote an agenda as legitimate news coverage,” Margolis said. “Still, this probably could’ve been handled better. The optics aren’t good. Picking a fight with the press corps this close to the midterms isn’t the message Trump’s team should want dominating the news cycle. It’s a distraction from arguments he could actually be winning.”

In his blog, Jonathan Turley argued “the odds are against the President.”

“In Sherrill v. Knight, the [Supreme Court] ruled that the First Amendment limited the right of the White House to arbitrarily deny a press pass to a journalist. Since that time, viewpoint discrimination has long been viewed as not a reasonable basis for exclusion,” Turley wrote. “In this case, the White House gave no procedural protections or any reason other than the President’s view that these outlets were publishing ‘fake news.’”

“The White House will have to argue that it can deny access without notice, procedural protections, and based entirely on the content of coverage. In other words, it will have to argue that it can engage in viewpoint discrimination,” Turley said. “This would create a dangerous and unfettered power. Future presidents could use it to bar conservative media and outlets that expose government abuse or waste. Whatever the outcome of this litigation, it is not a policy that advances our core values and traditions.”

What the left is saying.
  • The left opposes the ban, with some tying it to Trump’s past actions against the press.
  • Many argue the action violates the First Amendment.
  • Others suggest the move will backfire.

The New York Times editorial board said “Trump is attacking press freedom and disregarding the law.”

“Twice during President Trump’s first term, his administration tried to prevent a journalist whose work it did not like from reporting at the White House. Twice, judges rejected the moves as unconstitutional and restored the journalists’ access,” the board wrote. “Now the administration is attempting the same move, barring journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House because they had written what the president called ‘purposefully negative stories.’”

“The seemingly arcane question of which media organizations have access to the White House fits with a larger pattern of Mr. Trump’s attempts to control the media. Officials from his administration have searched the home of a Washington Post reporter and served subpoenas to staff members of The New York Times,” the board said. “He has impinged on press freedom in ways that no other modern president has. If he now gets away with punishing CNN, MS NOW and Politico, he will be able to credibly threaten other organizations.”

In MS NOW, Dan Froomkin called the action “Trump’s unconstitutional press ban.”

“Banning journalists won’t make the bad news go away. The media isn’t lying about the war Trump started in Iran, or the haphazard and nonsensical tariffs he imposed, or the grocery and gas prices,” Froomkin wrote. “And now, increasingly, unavoidably, Trump can see that more and more American voters are turning against him. The polls predicting Democratic success in the midterm elections must be weighing on him… But shooting the messenger never works. 

“And it likely won’t last, either. It is hard to imagine a more overt violation of the First Amendment than punishing journalists because he doesn’t like their coverage. That is a textbook example of viewpoint discrimination, which is unconstitutional,” Froomkin said. “This is a tired playbook that will do little to distract the nation’s focus from his dismal record and his failure to deliver on his biggest campaign promises: Stop the forever wars and bring down prices. And unfortunately for Trump, journalists can keep reporting on all those things, whether standing in the Oval Office or safely outside the Secret Service perimeter.”

In The Atlantic, Jonathan Chait argued “Trump’s attacks on the media are self-defeating.”

“Donald Trump is presiding over a failing presidency and lashing out at the news media — most recently by banning CNN, Politico, and MS NOW from the White House,” Chait wrote. “There might seem to be a connection between these two things, but the causal link is not that Trump is punishing the press because he is failing; rather, it’s the opposite. His inability to govern is in part a consequence of his hatred for the news media.”

“[Trump] has turned his party into a personality cult that disregards all evidence of failure. This project requires constant reminders that the hated press cannot be trusted, and that Trump himself is the source of all truth,” Chait said. “The most profound effect of his attacks has been to seal off many Republican minds from the fresh air of critique and correction. But the GOP’s efforts to discredit the media, rather than protecting the party from its own governing failures, have only made those failures worse.”

Many of these examples are deliberately misleading — like the case of an African journalist named Simon Ateba being “barred” by the Biden administration when, actually, he was denied a permanent hard pass but granted a day pass every time he requested one. 

Other defenders of the president argue that he has a right to ban these outlets because of their bias. “Reporters covering White House briefings should be conveying facts, not spin,” Ward Clark wrote in RedState. Ironically, if that’s true, then RedState’s own press credentials for the Pentagon and White House should be revoked immediately, given that — as their name implies — they are a news organization whose agenda is explicitly aligned with Trump’s.

Quotes like Clark’s make it exceedingly clear how silly and dangerous this all is. Every administration has its critics and allies in the press; this has been true since the Washington administration, and it should be true going forward. None have ever done what Trump is attempting to do now. Bias is in the eye of the beholder, which is precisely why nobody should support an administration banning news outlets it deems as biased — even if they have a track record of mistakes. All that does is ensure future administrations will further restrict press access they don’t like, which is a loss for anyone who believes in free exchange. 

It’s astonishing to me that the administration thinks this is the play right now. Yes, the media — writ large — is distrusted by the public and obsessed with itself and will inevitably devote plenty of coverage to its own lawsuits and fights with the administration. I’m sure some of them will even build subscription drives off the battle. That’s their right, and maybe Trump is just betting that CNN, MS NOW and Politico will spend more time on “resistance” navel-gazing and less time critically reporting on actual stories about his administration. 

But the knock-on effects are already breaking against him. Yesterday, the administration held an event so Trump could unveil his new helipad, but there was no audio on the televised event because there was no press pool after the other four networks, including Fox News, banded with CNN and against the ban. It was actually really encouraging to see Fox News's Washington bureau chief condemn the ban during his time as chair of the broadcasting consortium — a reminder that, despite our perceptions of these organizations as partisan warriors, they still lean on traditions of collegiality and mutual respect.

Hours later, Trump launched “Trump TV,” a 24/7 streaming show on the White House YouTube channel that purports to play the greatest hits of his administration, live updates, and breaking news. When I checked the channel out this morning, there was a grand total of 934 people watching a re-run of a Trump rally — and commenting was prohibited. This is the same administration that promised to “restore free speech.”

Really consider the context here: Gas and diesel prices are both significantly higher than they were when Biden left office, and rising. We’re still stuck in the Iran War, which is now spreading. The Russia–Ukraine war rages on. Inflation is higher today than it was when Biden left office. The number of uninsured Americans has gone up since Biden left office. The native-born employment rate is stagnant. Real wage gains are down, too. There is no long-promised healthcare bill, no election reform bill, no immigration reform bill. The House was just sent home after doing a grand total of four months of work this year because they didn’t want to take a tough vote on impeaching Trump’s secretary of Defense. Now, they won’t be back until after the midterms. 

If any of this concerns you, don’t worry; President Trump is focusing his time on what matters. He just got a new helipad at the White House. He’s hard at work building his ballroom and fighting to get his name on the Kennedy Center (or knock it down), and he’s got plans to turn his grand arch into a drone-deploying military station. And now, thankfully, he’s banned three news organizations from the White House who post stories he doesn’t like, which will inevitably result in taxpayer money being used to fight lawsuits from those organizations that he will very likely lose. 

If this is how the president thinks he can stave off a midterm blowout — or rescue his quickly sinking approval ratings — then the bubble he’s living in is farther removed from reality than I even thought. That’s bad news for Trump, worse news for us, and a much bigger deal than any of the shoddy reporting we’ve all had to live through over the last decade.
